newsitem.title: USA: SEC chief says decimal stock quotes inevitable.
newsitem.headline: SEC chief says decimal stock quotes inevitable.

text.p: Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt told key lawmakers that it makes sense for stocks to be traded in dollars and cents rather than in fractions.

"A transition to decimal pricing is both desirable and inevitable," Levitt wrote in May 19 letter to two key lawmakers, Representative John Dingell, a Michican Democrat and New York Democrat Thomas Manton. The letter was made available Tuesday.
Most stocks are traded in eighths or sixteenths of a dollar, so the smallest trading increment is either 12.5 cents or 6.25 cents, respectively.
Switching to decimals, could, in theory, allow these spreads to shrink to as little as one cent.

Levitt's comments stopped short of endorsing a bill that the House Commerce Committee's Finance and Hazardous Materials subcommittee will vote Wednesday that would move stock quoting in the United States to decimals from fractions.
"People are being eighthed and sixteenthed right out of their stock profits," said Michael Oxley, the Ohio Republican who chairs the subcommittee.
Oxley maintains that trading in dollars and cents would narrow spreads and could ultimately benefit American investors by as much as $2.5 billion annually.
His bill would call on the Securities and Exchange Commission to develop a plan within a year to move stock and options markets away from trading in fractions.

But Levitt noted that several market makers this month have narrowed their trading increments for New York Stock Exchange listed securities to sixteenths and thirty-seconds. The American Stock Exchange had made the shift as well.
"In light of these developments, it is even more likely that the industry, in time, will move to decimal pricing," Levitt wrote.
He warned that market players would need enough time to implement such a move.
Meanwhile, supporters of the legislation being considered say a shift to decimals from fractions would enable investors to save money in transaction costs.

The bi-partisan measure, introduced by Oxley and Massachusetts Democrat Edward Markey, is supported by Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican. However, some members of the panel have raised concerns about the legislation.
